stem: In Git, what is a branch such as `main` or `feature/login`?

options.text: A full copy of the project files stored in its own folder
options.why: Git never copies the tree per branch; switching branches rewrites the working tree from shared objects.

options.text: A movable pointer to a single commit, stored as a ref
options.why: A branch is just a name (in .git/refs/heads or packed-refs) holding one commit ID that moves forward as you commit.

options.text: A list of the commit IDs that belong only to that branch
options.why: Git stores no per-branch commit list; which commits are "on" a branch is computed by walking parents from its tip.

options.text: A separate repository linked to the original by a remote
options.why: That describes a fork or clone, not a branch inside one repository.

explanation: A branch is a lightweight ref: a name that holds one commit ID. Committing on the branch writes a new commit whose parent is the old tip and then moves the ref to it. The commits "on" a branch are simply those reachable by following parent links from its tip, which is why creating a branch is instant and costs almost nothing.
reference: Pro Git: Branches in a Nutshell

stem: Running `git diff` with no arguments shows the changes you have already staged with `git add`.

options.why: Plain `git diff` compares the working tree with the index, so staged changes do not appear in it.
It shows unstaged changes only; use `git diff --staged` (or `--cached`) for what is staged.

explanation: Git has three states for a change: modified in the working tree, staged in the index, and committed. `git diff` shows working tree vs index, so once you `git add` a change it disappears from that output. `git diff --staged` shows index vs HEAD, and `git diff HEAD` shows both together.

stem: You staged some edits and want to review exactly what the next `git commit` will record. Which command shows that?

options.why: This compares the working tree with the index, so it shows what is not yet staged.
With no argument it shows the last commit, not what is about to be committed.
It compares the index with HEAD, which is exactly the content of the next commit.
This prints the patches of commits that already exist in history.

explanation: The next commit is built from the index, so the diff between HEAD and the index is what will be recorded. `git diff --staged` (synonym `--cached`) shows it. Unstaged edits still in the working tree are not included unless you add them first.

stem: Git records what HEAD currently points to (usually a line like `ref: refs/heads/main`) in a file directly inside the `.git` directory. Type the name of that file.
explanation: `.git/HEAD` normally contains a symbolic ref such as `ref: refs/heads/main`, meaning HEAD follows that branch. In detached HEAD state the file holds a raw commit ID instead. `git symbolic-ref HEAD` prints the branch it follows and fails when HEAD is detached.

stem: What does `git log --oneline` print for each commit?

options.text: The full 40-character hash and the author email
options.why: It abbreviates the hash and does not print the email.

options.text: An abbreviated hash followed by the commit subject
options.why: `--oneline` is shorthand for `--pretty=oneline --abbrev-commit`.

options.text: The commit subject followed by the list of changed files
options.why: Changed files need `--stat` or `--name-only`; oneline shows no file list.

options.text: The author name and date followed by the subject
options.why: Author and date are part of the default format, not the oneline format.

explanation: `git log --oneline` gives one line per commit: a short hash and the first line of the message. Add `--graph` to draw branch structure, `--decorate` (on by default in terminals) to show branch and tag names, and `--all` to include every ref.

stem: Match each command with what it shows.

options.text: Files changed in each commit, with insertion and deletion counts
options.why: This is the --stat summary.

options.text: One commit's message and its patch
options.why: This is what git show prints.

options.text: The commit that last changed each line of a file
options.why: This is git blame.

options.text: Number of commits per author, sorted by count
options.why: This is git shortlog -sn.

explanation: `--stat` adds a per-file change summary to each logged commit. `git show` prints one object, for a commit its metadata plus patch. `git blame` annotates each line with the commit and author that last touched it. `git shortlog -s -n` summarises commit counts per author, sorted numerically.

stem: What does it mean when Git says you are in "detached HEAD" state?

options.text: The repository has lost its connection to the remote
options.why: Remotes are unrelated to HEAD; detached HEAD is purely local.

options.text: HEAD points to a branch that has been deleted
options.why: Deleting the current branch is refused; detached means HEAD names no branch at all.

options.text: HEAD points directly at a commit instead of at a branch
options.why: New commits then move only HEAD, and no branch name follows them.

options.text: The working tree has uncommitted changes that block switching
options.why: That is a separate situation; detached HEAD can have a clean tree.

explanation: Normally HEAD is a symbolic ref to a branch, and committing moves that branch. After checking out a commit ID, a tag or a remote-tracking branch, HEAD holds a commit ID directly. You can look around and even commit, but those commits are reachable only through HEAD until you create a branch for them.

stem: Which commands leave you in detached HEAD state? (Choose two.)

options.why: Checking out a raw commit ID points HEAD at that commit, not at a branch.
Tags are not branches, so HEAD is detached at the tagged commit.
Switching to a local branch makes HEAD follow that branch.
This creates a new branch and attaches HEAD to it.
Committing on a branch moves the branch; HEAD stays attached.

explanation: HEAD detaches whenever you check out something that is not a local branch: a commit ID, a tag, a remote-tracking branch like `origin/main`, or `git switch --detach`. `git switch` refuses non-branch targets unless you pass `--detach`, which makes the state change explicit.

stem: You append line `d` to `f.txt` and run `git add f.txt`, then append line `e` without staging it. What does `git diff HEAD` show?

options.text: Only `e`, because staged changes are hidden from `git diff`
options.why: That is the plain `git diff` (working tree vs index); adding HEAD changes the comparison.

options.text: Only `d`, because HEAD refers to what is staged
options.why: HEAD is the last commit; the staged view needs `--staged`.

options.text: Both `d` and `e`: working tree compared with HEAD
options.why: It skips the index and shows everything changed since HEAD.

options.text: Nothing, because the file has both staged and unstaged edits
options.why: Mixed states are normal; each diff form just compares different snapshots.

explanation: There are three snapshots: HEAD, the index and the working tree. `git diff` compares working tree to index (only `e`), `git diff --staged` compares index to HEAD (only `d`), and `git diff HEAD` compares working tree to HEAD (both lines). Running the scenario gives numstat counts of 1, 1 and 2 lines added.

stem:
Given this history, which commits does `git log --format=%s main..feature` list?

```text
* C        (main)
| * Y     (feature)
| * X
|/
* B
* A
```

options.why: Two dots list commits reachable from feature but not from main.
That is `feature..main`: commits on main that feature lacks.
That set is the three-dot symmetric difference, `main...feature`.
`B` and `A` are reachable from main too, so they are excluded.

explanation: In log and rev-list, `A..B` means "reachable from B but not from A", the same as `B ^A`. So `main..feature` lists the commits the feature branch would bring to main: `Y` and `X`. Reversing the operands lists what main has that feature lacks.

stem:
With the same history, what does `git log --format=%s main...feature` list?

```text
* C        (main)
| * Y     (feature)
| * X
|/
* B
* A
```

options.why: That is the two-dot range `main..feature`.
Three dots give commits reachable from either side but not both.
The merge base is excluded; `git merge-base` is the command that prints it.
Commits reachable from both branches, `B` and `A`, are left out.

explanation: In log, `A...B` is the symmetric difference: commits reachable from exactly one of the two refs. Here that is `C` from main plus `X` and `Y` from feature. Adding `--left-right` marks which side each commit came from.

stem: `git diff main..feature` compares the tip of `feature` with the merge base of the two branches, just as the two-dot range does in `git log`.

options.why: In `git diff` two dots are just shorthand for comparing the two tips directly.
`git diff main..feature` equals `git diff main feature`; the merge-base form is three dots.

explanation: Range syntax means different things in diff and log. `git diff A..B` is the same as `git diff A B`: tip against tip, so it also shows main's own changes in reverse. `git diff A...B` diffs from the merge base of A and B to B, which is what a pull request shows. In the test repo, `..` listed `f.txt` (changed only on main) while `...` listed only `x.txt`.

stem:
In this history, which commit does `HEAD^2` refer to?

```text
*   M      (main, HEAD)
|\
| * Y     (feature)
| * X
* | C
|/
* B
* A
```
`M` was created by running `git merge feature` while on `main`.

options.why: `C` is the first parent, `HEAD^` or `HEAD^1`.
`^2` selects the second parent, the tip of the branch that was merged in.
`B` is two first-parent steps back, `HEAD~2`.
`X` is one step behind the second parent, `HEAD^2~1`.

explanation: `^n` picks the n-th parent of a commit. A merge made on main records main's previous tip as parent 1 and the merged branch tip as parent 2, so `HEAD^2` is `Y`. `~n` always follows first parents, which is why `HEAD~2` is `B` here.

stem:
In this history, which commit is `HEAD~2`?

```text
*   M      (main, HEAD)
|\
| * Y     (feature)
| * X
* | C
|/
* B
* A
```
`M` was created by running `git merge feature` while on `main`.

options.why: Reaching `X` needs the second parent, `HEAD^2~1`.
`Y` is the second parent of `M`, `HEAD^2`.
`~2` follows first parents twice: `M` to `C` to `B`.
`A` is `HEAD~3`.

explanation: `~n` means "the n-th generation ancestor, following only first parents". From `M` the first parent is `C`, and its parent is `B`. Use `^2` to step into the merged branch, then `~` to walk it.

stem: A commit adds two different files, `a.txt` and `b.txt`, each containing exactly the text `hello` followed by a newline. How many blob objects does Git store for their contents? Type a number.
explanation: Blobs are content-addressed: the object ID is a hash of the content, not the file name. Both files hash to the same blob (`ce013625…` for "hello\n"), so Git stores it once. File names live in the tree object, which has two entries pointing at that one blob.

stem: You renamed `a.py` to `b.py` with `git mv` and committed. Now `git log -- b.py` lists only the rename commit. How do you see the history from before the rename too?

options.why: `--all` adds every ref, but the path filter still stops at the rename.
This mixes both paths' commits but does not track the content across renames.
`--follow` keeps tracking the file's content across renames.
`--stat` only adds change counts; it does not widen the history.

explanation: Git records no rename metadata; a rename is a delete plus an add that diff tools detect by similarity. A plain path filter therefore stops where `b.py` first appears. `git log --follow` (single file only) detects the rename and continues with the old name; in the test repo it listed all four commits instead of one.

stem: Which commands list commits that are on `main` but not on `feature`? (Choose three.)

options.why: Reachable from main, excluding anything reachable from feature.
The `^` prefix excludes everything reachable from feature.
`--not` negates the refs that follow it, the same as `^`.
This is the opposite direction: commits on feature that main lacks.
Three dots include commits unique to either side, not just main.

explanation: `feature..main`, `main ^feature` and `main --not feature` are three spellings of the same set: commits reachable from main minus those reachable from feature. The order of the two-dot operands matters, and the three-dot form is a symmetric difference.

stem: Put the objects in the order Git follows them to read the contents of `README.md` on the `main` branch.

options.why: Last: the blob stores the bytes.
First: the branch name resolves to a commit ID.
Second: it names the root tree and the parents.
Third: its entries map names like README.md to blobs.

explanation: A branch ref holds a commit ID. The commit points to one root tree (plus parent commits and metadata). The tree lists names, modes and object IDs, and the entry for README.md points to a blob with the file's content. `git cat-file -p main`, then `-p <tree>`, then `-p <blob>` walks the same path.

stem: Which commits does `git log --author="Ana"` select?

options.text: Only those whose author name is exactly `Ana`
options.why: The value is a regular expression matched anywhere, not an exact name.

options.text: Those that Ana committed, even if someone else authored them
options.why: That is `--committer`; `--author` checks the author field.

options.text: Those whose author ident matches the regex, e.g. `Anand` too
options.why: The pattern is a regex searched in the author ident, so substrings match.
Messages are searched with `--grep`, not `--author`.

explanation: `--author` and `--committer` take a regular expression matched against the whole ident line, which includes the name and email. "Ana" therefore also matches "Anand" or an email containing "Ana". Anchor or extend the pattern (for example `--author="^Ana <"`) when you need an exact person. Matching is case-sensitive unless you add `-i`.

stem: A commit changed `total = calc(1)` to `total = calc(2)`. `git log -S calc --oneline` does not list that commit, but `git log -G calc --oneline` does. Why?

options.text: `-S` only searches commit messages, while `-G` searches the patch text itself
options.why: Both look at diffs; messages are searched with `--grep`.

options.text: `-S` counts occurrences, which stayed the same; `-G` matches changed lines
options.why: The edit kept one occurrence, so the count was unchanged.

options.text: `-S` ignores commits that modify a line instead of adding one
options.why: It does not care about line types, only the occurrence count.
Neither is case-insensitive unless you add `-i`.

explanation: The pickaxe `-S<string>` finds commits that change how many times the string occurs, which makes it ideal for "when was this function added or removed?". `-G<regex>` finds commits whose added or removed lines match the regex, even if the count stays the same. In the test repo `-S calc` listed only the first commit, while `-G calc` listed both.

stem:
On this history, what does `git log --first-parent --format=%s` list?

```text
*   M      (main, HEAD)
|\
| * Y     (feature)
| * X
* | C
|/
* B
* A
```
`M` was created by running `git merge feature` while on `main`.

options.why: That is the full history; first-parent skips the merged branch.
Merge commits stay in the output; only their side branches are skipped.
It follows only first parents from M, so X and Y are not visited.
That would follow second parents instead.

explanation: `--first-parent` walks only the first parent of each merge, giving the mainline as it looked on the branch where merges happened: each merged feature appears as one merge commit. This is handy for release notes and for bisecting at merge granularity. Running it on the test repo printed M, C, B, A.

stem:
In this history, which commit does `HEAD^2~1` refer to?

```text
*   M      (main, HEAD)
|\
| * Y     (feature)
| * X
* | C
|/
* B
* A
```
`M` was created by running `git merge feature` while on `main`.

options.why: Second parent of M is Y, and one first-parent step back from Y is X.
`C` is `HEAD^1`, reached without entering the merged branch.
`B` is `HEAD~2`, the first-parent route.
`Y` is `HEAD^2` itself; `~1` moves one more step back.

explanation: Revision suffixes apply left to right. `HEAD^2` selects M's second parent, Y. `~1` then takes Y's first parent, X. Combining `^` to choose a branch at a merge with `~` to walk it lets you name any commit relative to HEAD.

stem:
HEAD is the merge commit `M` below. Which revisions resolve to commit `C`? (Choose three.)

```text
*   M      (main, HEAD)
|\
| * Y     (feature)
| * X
* | C
|/
* B
* A
```
`M` was created by running `git merge feature` while on `main`.

options.why: A bare `^` means the first parent, which is C.
One first-parent step from M is C.
Parent number 1 of M is C, main's tip before the merge.
The second parent is Y, the merged branch tip.
Two first-parent steps reach B.

explanation: `HEAD^`, `HEAD^1` and `HEAD~1` all mean the first parent. They diverge only when you go further: `^2` picks another parent of the same commit, while `~2` goes two generations back along first parents.

stem: You make a commit in detached HEAD state and then run `git switch main`. Git deletes that commit straight away, because no branch points to it.

options.why: Git only warns that the commit is being left behind; nothing is deleted at that moment.
The commit becomes unreachable from branches but stays in the object store and the HEAD reflog until garbage collection expires it.

explanation: On switching away Git prints "you are leaving 1 commit behind, not connected to any of your branches" with the commit ID. The object still exists, and HEAD's reflog records it (for example `HEAD@{1}`), so `git branch keep <id>` recovers it. It is only pruned by `git gc` after its reflog entry expires (30 days by default for unreachable entries).

stem: What exactly does `git diff main...feature` compare?

options.text: The tips of `main` and `feature` against each other
options.why: That is `git diff main feature` or `main..feature`.

options.text: The merge base against the tip of `feature`
options.why: It shows only what changed on feature since the branches diverged.

options.text: Every commit on either branch since they diverged, one at a time
options.why: `git diff` produces one combined diff, not a per-commit listing.

options.text: The tip of `main` against the merge base
options.why: That would be `git diff feature...main`.

explanation: `git diff A...B` is shorthand for `git diff $(git merge-base A B) B`. It isolates the changes made on B, ignoring whatever happened on A meanwhile, which is why review tools use it. In the test repo it listed only `x.txt`, while the two-dot form also listed `f.txt`, changed only on main.

stem: A Prettier commit reformatted every line of `api.ts`, changing quotes and line wrapping. Now `git blame api.ts` attributes nearly every line to that commit. How do you get useful blame output while keeping the formatting commit?

options.text: Run `git blame -w api.ts` to ignore the formatting changes
options.why: `-w` ignores whitespace only; changed quotes and re-wrapped lines still count.

options.text: Add its hash to `.git-blame-ignore-revs` and use it
options.why: Blame then passes through that commit and credits the lines to earlier authors.

options.text: Run `git blame -M api.ts` so moved lines are tracked
options.why: `-M` detects lines moved within the file; reformatted lines still differ.
`--reverse` shows when lines were last present, not who wrote them.

explanation: `git blame --ignore-rev <hash>`, or a list file used via `--ignore-revs-file` or `blame.ignoreRevsFile`, makes blame skip bulk mechanical commits and attribute lines to the change before them. GitHub's blame view also honours a `.git-blame-ignore-revs` file at the repository root. `-w` only helps when the noise is pure whitespace.

stem: A developer moved a 40-line function from `utils.js` into `helpers.js` in one commit. `git blame helpers.js` now shows that developer for all 40 lines. Which option makes blame credit the original authors?

options.why: Whitespace is not the issue; the lines were moved between files.
`-M` finds lines moved within the same file only.
`-C` also detects lines moved or copied from other files changed in the same commit.
`-L` limits the line range but does not look across files.

explanation: `git blame -C` searches other files modified in the same commit for the origin of moved or copied lines, so the moved function is credited to whoever originally wrote it. Repeating it (`-C -C`, `-C -C -C`) widens the search to the commit that created the file and then to any commit, at extra cost.

stem: What does `git log -L :parsePrice:src/money.js` show?

options.text: Every commit that touched `src/money.js`, with full patches
options.why: A plain path filter would do that; `-L` narrows to one function.

options.text: Each commit that changed `parsePrice`, with diffs limited to it
options.why: `-L :<funcname>:<file>` traces the evolution of that line range.

options.text: The line numbers where `parsePrice` is called across the repository
options.why: That is a search task for `git grep`.

options.text: The author of each line of `parsePrice` at HEAD
options.why: That would be `git blame -L`, which annotates rather than lists history.

explanation: Line-range log traces a region through history. `-L <start>,<end>:<file>` follows explicit line numbers, and `-L :<funcname>:<file>` uses a function-name regex to find the region. Each listed commit shows a patch restricted to that range, which is often the fastest way to answer "how did this function change?".

stem: Match each revision expression with what it means.

options.text: The upstream (tracking) branch of the current branch
options.why: For example origin/main.

options.text: The branch you were on before the last checkout or switch
options.why: Same as `git switch -`.

options.text: Where `main` pointed two updates ago, from its reflog
options.why: Reflog position, not ancestry.

options.text: The tree object of the commit HEAD points to
options.why: Peels the commit to its tree.

explanation: `@{u}` (or `@{upstream}`) names the configured upstream. `@{-N}` is the N-th previously checked-out branch. `ref@{N}` reads the ref's reflog, so it tracks what the ref pointed at over time rather than parent relationships. `<rev>^{type}` peels an object to the given type, such as a commit's tree or a tag's commit.

stem: On `main` (tip `C`), you run `git merge feature`, which creates merge commit `M`. What does `ORIG_HEAD` point to afterwards?

options.why: That is HEAD; ORIG_HEAD keeps the previous position.
The merged branch tip is MERGE_HEAD during a merge, not ORIG_HEAD.

options.text: The merge base of the two merged branches
options.why: Git does not store the merge base in a ref.

options.text: `C`, where main was before the merge
options.why: Merge records the old HEAD in ORIG_HEAD so you can return to it.

explanation: Commands that move HEAD drastically (merge, rebase, reset, pull) save the previous HEAD in `ORIG_HEAD`. After a merge, `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` undoes it. In the test repo `git log -1 ORIG_HEAD` printed `C` after the merge.

stem: You create a tag with `git tag -a v1 -m "release"`. What does `git cat-file -t v1` print? Type the single word.
explanation: An annotated tag is its own object of type `tag`, holding the tagger, date, message (and optional signature) plus a pointer to the commit. A lightweight tag (`git tag v1-light`) is just a ref to the commit, so `git cat-file -t v1-light` prints `commit`. Both outputs were confirmed in a test repo.

stem: A commit was authored in 2020 but rebased onto `main` last week. Why does `git log --since="2 weeks ago"` still list it?

options.text: `--since` lists any commit reachable from a recently updated branch
options.why: It filters each commit by date, not by when a ref last moved.

options.text: `--since` compares against the latest reflog entry of HEAD
options.why: Reflog dates are not used for this filter.

options.text: It filters on committer date, and the rebase set a new one
options.why: Rebasing rewrites commits, giving them a new committer date while keeping the author date.

options.text: `--since` is ignored unless you also pass `--until`
options.why: Either limit works on its own.

explanation: Every commit has an author date (when the change was first written) and a committer date (when this commit object was created). `--since`/`--until` limit by committer date, so rebased, cherry-picked or amended commits look new. A test commit with author date 2020 and committer date 2026 appeared under `--since=2026-09-01`. Print both with `--format="%ad %cd"`.

stem: Which statements about how Git handles renamed files are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Git stores no rename record; renames are inferred by comparing content
options.why: A commit only has trees, so renames are detected when diffing.

options.text: By default, a deleted and an added file are paired as a rename at 50% similarity
options.why: The default `-M` threshold is 50%, tunable with `-M<n>`.

options.text: `git mv` writes a special rename entry into the commit
options.why: `git mv` is a convenience for mv + rm + add; nothing special is recorded.

options.text: A file's earlier history is lost once it is renamed
options.why: Nothing is lost; you just need `--follow` to see it under the old name.

options.text: Rename detection is off unless you configure `diff.renames`
options.why: It has been on by default for diff and log since Git 2.9.

explanation: Git snapshots trees, so a rename is just "old path gone, new path present". Diff, log, merge and blame detect renames by content similarity (50% by default). This works the same whether you used `git mv` or plain `mv` plus `git add -A`. Large edits made in the same commit as a rename can drop similarity below the threshold, so commit renames separately when you can.

stem:
You commit `N` on top of merge commit `M` below, so `N` is now HEAD. Which commit does `HEAD~1^2` refer to?

```text
*   M      (main, HEAD)
|\
| * Y     (feature)
| * X
* | C
|/
* B
* A
```
`M` was created by running `git merge feature` while on `main`.

options.why: `HEAD~1^1` would give C; `^2` takes the other parent.
`HEAD~1` alone is M; the `^2` step continues from there.
X is one step further, `HEAD~1^2~1`.
HEAD~1 is M, and M's second parent is Y.

explanation: Evaluate suffixes left to right. `HEAD~1` moves from N to its first parent M. `^2` then selects M's second parent, the tip of the merged feature branch, Y. Mixing `~` and `^` lets you name any commit relative to HEAD without copying hashes.

stem: Before opening a pull request, you run `git diff main..feature` to review your branch. It shows changes to `f.txt`, which your branch never touched; someone changed it on `main` after you branched. What is going on?

options.text: In diff, `..` compares the two tips, so main's changes appear reversed
options.why: Use `git diff main...feature` to diff from the merge base, as pull requests do.

options.text: Git attributes the change to your branch because the file shares an ancestor
options.why: Diff compares snapshots; it attributes nothing to anyone.

options.text: Your branch silently picked up main's commits when you last fetched
options.why: Fetching updates remote-tracking refs, not your branch.

options.text: Two dots exclude the merge base, so its files are shown as changed
options.why: The merge base plays no part in the two-dot diff at all.

explanation: `git diff main..feature` is `git diff main feature`: snapshot against snapshot. Anything main changed since the branch point shows up as if your branch undid it. `git diff main...feature` diffs from `git merge-base main feature` to feature, isolating your work, which is what GitHub's "Files changed" tab shows. In a test repo the two-dot form listed `f.txt` and `x.txt`; the three-dot form listed only `x.txt`.

stem:
Before the merge, the history looked like this. What does `git log --left-right --format="%m %s" main...feature` print?

```text
* C        (main)
| * Y     (feature)
| * X
|/
* B
* A
```

options.why: The arrows point the other way: `<` marks the left operand, main.
C is reachable only from the left side (main), and X and Y only from the right.
B is reachable from both sides, so the symmetric difference drops it.
That ignores main's unique commit C, which three dots include.

explanation: With a symmetric difference `L...R`, `--left-right` marks each commit with `<` if it is reachable only from L and `>` if only from R; `%m` prints that mark. This shows at a glance how two branches diverged. Adding `--cherry-pick` also hides commits whose patches exist on both sides. Running this on the test repo printed `< C`, `> Y`, `> X`.

stem: A commit is no longer reachable from any branch or tag. What keeps it from being removed by the next `git gc`?

options.text: Nothing; `git gc` deletes every unreachable object immediately
options.why: gc honours reflogs and a grace period for loose objects.

options.text: The fact that it is stored in a pack file rather than loose
options.why: Packing does not protect unreachable objects; repacking drops them.

options.text: A reflog entry that still references it
options.why: Reflogs count as roots until they expire, 30 days for unreachable entries.

options.text: Its author date being newer than `gc.pruneExpire`
options.why: Prune age is based on the object file's age, not commit dates.

explanation: Garbage collection keeps everything reachable from refs and from reflog entries. Reflog entries for commits no longer reachable from the ref expire after `gc.reflogExpireUnreachable` (30 days by default); reachable ones last 90. Only then can objects become prunable, and loose ones also get `gc.pruneExpire` grace (2 weeks). This is why "lost" commits are usually recoverable through the reflog.

stem: You edit two files, run `git add .`, then `git commit -m "fix"`. Put the steps in the order Git writes or updates things.

options.text: The branch ref (for example refs/heads/main) moves to the new commit
options.why: Last: the branch is only updated once the commit object exists.

options.text: Blob objects for the new file contents are written
options.why: First: `git add` hashes the content and stores blobs.

options.text: A commit object pointing to the root tree and parent is written
options.why: Third: it records the tree, parent, author, committer and message.

options.text: Tree objects are written from the index
options.why: Second: `git commit` turns the index into a tree hierarchy.

explanation: `git add` writes blobs and records them in the index. `git commit` writes the trees that the index describes, then a commit object referencing the root tree and the previous HEAD as parent, and finally moves the current branch (and the HEAD reflog) to the new commit. Because the ref update happens last, an interrupted commit never leaves a branch pointing at a half-written commit.

stem: A teammate merged `main` into their feature branch to resolve conflicts, then pushed that merge commit directly as the new `main` (a fast-forward). Now `git log --first-parent main` walks the feature branch's commits instead of the old mainline. Why?

options.text: Fast-forward pushes rewrite the parent order of the commits they move
options.why: Commits are immutable; a push only moves a ref.

options.text: Its first parent is the feature tip, so first-parent follows feature
options.why: Merging main into feature made feature parent 1; fast-forwarding made it main's new tip.

options.text: `--first-parent` always prefers the parent with more commits
options.why: It always takes parent 1, whatever the branch sizes.

options.text: Git reorders parents by commit date when computing first-parent
options.why: Parent order is fixed when the merge is created.

explanation: The first parent of a merge is whatever HEAD was when the merge was made. Merging main into feature records feature as parent 1. When that merge is fast-forwarded onto main (sometimes called a "foxtrot merge"), main's first-parent chain detours through the feature branch, breaking first-parent logs and bisects. Teams avoid it by merging feature into main (for example via pull requests) instead of fast-forwarding to such commits.

stem: `git branch` lists `release/1.2`, but there is no file `.git/refs/heads/release/1.2`. The repository is not corrupted. Where is the ref stored?

options.why: The index tracks file staging, not branch refs.

options.text: Only in the HEAD reflog under `.git/logs`
options.why: Reflogs record history but do not define refs.
That section holds tracking settings, not the commit ID.
Packed refs are stored one per line in a single file.

explanation: To avoid thousands of tiny files, Git can move refs into `.git/packed-refs` (`git pack-refs --all`, run by `git gc`). When a packed ref is next updated, Git writes a loose file for it, and loose refs take precedence over packed entries. Scripts should therefore read refs with `git rev-parse` or `git for-each-ref`, never by opening files. Newer Git can also use the reftable backend instead of files.

stem: If you recreate a commit with the same tree, parents, author and message, but at a later time so the committer timestamp differs, it gets the same commit hash as the original.

options.why: The timestamps are part of the hashed commit object, so changing one changes the ID.
The commit ID hashes every header, including the committer date, so it changes.

explanation: A commit's ID is the hash of its full content: tree, parent IDs, author line with timestamp, committer line with timestamp, and message. Change any of them and you get a different commit, which is why amending, rebasing or cherry-picking always produces new IDs even when the code is identical. `git cat-file -p HEAD` shows exactly what is hashed.

stem: For release notes you want one line per merged feature plus any direct commits on `main`, but none of the individual commits inside merged feature branches. Which command gives that?

options.why: This drops merge commits and still lists every feature commit.
This lists only merges, losing the direct commits on main.
Excluding one branch's history does not hide other merged branches.
It walks only main's own line: merges appear once, their branches are skipped.

explanation: `--first-parent` follows main's mainline, so each merged feature shows up as its merge commit and direct commits appear as themselves. `--no-merges` does nearly the opposite: it removes merge commits while still listing everything inside the merged branches. On the test repo, first-parent printed M, C, B, A, while `--no-merges` printed five commits including X and Y.

stem:
HEAD is the merge commit `M` below. What number does `git rev-list --count HEAD` print? Type a number.

```text
*   M      (main, HEAD)
|\
| * Y     (feature)
| * X
* | C
|/
* B
* A
```
`M` was created by running `git merge feature` while on `main`.
explanation: `rev-list --count` counts every commit reachable from HEAD through all parents: M, C, Y, X, B and A, which makes 6. With `--first-parent` it would count 4 (M, C, B, A). This difference catches people who use the count as a "build number" on branches with merges. The test repo printed 6.

stem: Right after running `git reset --hard HEAD~3`, which statement about `HEAD@{1}` and `HEAD~1` is correct?

options.text: They are the same commit, because both mean "one step back"
options.why: They use different axes: reflog history versus ancestry.

options.text: `HEAD@{1}`: HEAD before the reset; `HEAD~1`: the new HEAD's parent
options.why: `@{n}` reads the reflog, while `~n` walks commit parents.

options.text: `HEAD@{1}` is HEAD's parent; `HEAD~1` is the commit before the reset
options.why: This swaps the two meanings.

options.text: `HEAD@{1}` no longer exists, because `--hard` clears the reflog
options.why: Reset adds a reflog entry; it never clears it.

explanation: `ref@{n}` means "what ref pointed to n moves ago" according to its reflog, so after the reset `HEAD@{1}` is the old tip three commits ahead. `ref~n` follows parent links from the current commit. That is why `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` undoes the reset, while `HEAD~1` would move further back.

stem: `M` merged `feature` into `main` with no conflicts. Which statements about inspecting `M` are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: `git show M` displays no diff hunks for a clean merge
options.why: Its combined diff only shows hunks that differ from every parent.

options.text: `git diff M^1 M` shows everything the merge brought into main
options.why: Diffing against the first parent shows the merge's net effect on main.

options.text: `git show M` prints the full diff against the first parent by default
options.why: The default for merges is the dense combined diff, not a first-parent diff.

options.text: A merge commit has no tree of its own; it reuses its parents' trees
options.why: Every commit, including merges, records exactly one root tree.

options.text: `git show` refuses to display merge commits
options.why: It shows them, with combined-diff output.

explanation: For merges, `git show` uses the dense combined diff (`--cc`), which hides any hunk that matches at least one parent. A clean merge therefore shows only its message; the test repo printed no diff lines. To see what the merge contributed to main, diff against the first parent (`git diff M^1 M`, or `git show --first-parent M` / `--diff-merges=first-parent`).
reference: git-show and git-log documentation: Diff Merges
